At the moment of hatching, these altricial nestlings weigh a meager 12.9 grams [Ww0 = 12.9 grams], a value that reflects the relatively small investment per offspring typical of many passerines that produce multiple broods. This initial wet weight serves as the baseline from which the dramatic growth trajectory of this species proceeds. The first phase of independence, marked by fledging, occurs relatively rapidly. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the species' active metabolic period (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), the nestling period concludes with fledging at 18.5 days after hatching [tx = 18.5 days after hatching]. This brief interval in the nest is typical of many paradise birds, where the pressure to minimize predation risk during the vulnerable nestling stage is high. Following fledging, the young bird enters a juvenile phase that will last until it attains its full adult body mass and reproductive capacity.

The intervening sub-adult period is characterized by continued somatic growth and the gradual acquisition of adult feathering, a process that demands sustained energy intake without the added metabolic burden of egg production or chick provisioning.

Adult body size in this species exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism, consistent with the polygynous mating system typical of birds of paradise. Males attain a significantly larger ultimate wet weight, reaching an average of 218.75 grams [Wwi = 218.75 grams], whereas females plateau at a lower adult mass of 207.5 grams [Wwi = 207.5 grams]. The reported range for males extends from 164 to 265 grams, while females generally fall between 160 and 255 grams, indicating substantial individual variation likely influenced by local resource availability. This size disparity is reflected in their foraging ecology and social interactions, with larger males often dominating access to fruiting trees in the rainforest canopy. Respirometry trials conducted under carefully controlled laboratory conditions have provided detailed insights into the basal metabolic rate of this species. The measurements were taken from post-absorptive, resting individuals during their inactive phase to ensure that the values represented true basal metabolism rather than activity-related energy expenditure. These data are essential for constructing accurate energy budgets for this species in its native lowland forest habitat.
